data.turoyo: Xori Brahim: Lo. Məštaʕenawo, Ǧan. Naṭtat nayṭinawo. Bi čərre məštaʕenawo. Bu məzid ʕal ḥaṣe d ḥḏoḏe qəbzinawo.
data.translation: Chorepiscopus Brahim: No. We used to play, Jan. We used to jump jumps. We used to play marbles. At leapfrog we used to jump onto one another's backs.

rationale: New I Infectum-wa box; first-person plural habitual play, cognate naṭtat and leapfrog path in the same self-contained context. English: supplied Jan machine translation.

data.turoyo: D dayšət ʕal u xəṭuṭano, gədnayṭət ʕal ḥaṣe. <...>
data.translation: If you step on this line, you will leap over his back. <...>

rationale: Thin I Infectum sense 1; overt gəd- prospect and path phrase in a complete condition. English: supplied Jan machine translation.

data.turoyo: Kowe ṭəworo bu lišono. Naqla ḥreto kduʕarno, kəmarno: ‘u kṯawbonoyo‘ uʕdo bu šəkəl d latlan darbo aw naṭṭa d nayṭina d məṭenale, kfašlan aḥna u lišonano di ǧġaliye, xəd gəšro, xəd dawse d əzzano lu kṯawbonoyo yo.
data.translation: Development takes place in the language. Once again I return and say: 'the literary language', now, since we have no way or leap by which to jump to reach it, this spoken language remains for us as a bridge, as steps by which to go to the literary language.

rationale: First example for figurative I.2; full language-development contrast distinguishes a denied direct leap from bridge/stepwise access. English: supplied Jan machine translation.

summary: One new masculine singular Preterit Intransitive context complements inherited feminine nayiṭo and plural nayiṭi; all retain sense 1.
Animate leaping, body parts displaced by a blow, and fire spreading across share the entry's established jump uses. The fire subject is already exemplified; no new sense or idiom is needed.
The source portion about the marten's leg has no counterpart in the supplied translation, so the added quotation starts at Nayəṭ and marks the cut.

Jan adds habitual play to the already established physical jumping sense and documents Infectum-wa. naṭtat is a cognate event noun and tloṯ dawsat measures extent; neither alone establishes a transitive lexical meaning.

The literary-language discussion supplies a clear figurative developmental leap. The clause denies the availability of a direct leap; the new sense does not assert that such a leap actually occurred. Path ʕal ḥaṣe remains ordinary physical motion in the play descriptions.
